summary: This memo proposes a protocol that, given a TCP port pair, returns a string naming the owner of that connection on the server's system. Suggested uses include identifying users during FTP sessions. It was replaced by RFC 931.

plainLanguage.summary: You ask a computer, "Who is using this connection?" and it answers with a name. This was an early try at that idea.

questions: what is the early authentication service protocol
how to identify the user of a tcp connection
how do you query the authentication server

subtitle: Query a server to learn who owns a TCP connection

tldr.problem: When a connection is made between two hosts, there is no standard way to ask a server who owns the connection on that server's side.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 912 proposes a service on TCP port 113 that accepts a query specifying a port pair and returns the user identifier owning that connection.
tldr.outcome: This approach was superseded by RFC 931, which is still used today as the Ident protocol.

facts.label: Protocol
facts.value: TCP connection-based, text query and response

today: RFC 912 was replaced by RFC 931 with refinements, establishing what became known as the Ident protocol.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 912 proposes the Authentication Service, which provides a way to determine the identity of a user on a TCP connection. Given a pair of TCP port numbers (local and foreign), an authentication server returns a character string identifying the owner of that connection on the server's system.

Suggested uses include automatic user identification during FTP sessions, additional verification for dial-up users, and access verification for network file servers. The motivation was personal: the author designed this protocol to avoid having to identify himself each time he used FTP.
sections.plainLanguage: The service lets you find out who is on the other end of a connection by asking the remote computer.

sections.title: Query and Response Format
sections.content:
A client establishes a TCP connection to the authentication server's port 113 (decimal) and sends a simple query of the form <local-port>, <foreign-port>, where <local-port> is the TCP port on the target (server) system and <foreign-port> is the TCP port on the source (client) system. For example, a query might be 23, 6191 to ask about a Telnet connection.

The server responds with <local-port>, <foreign-port> : <response-type> : <additional-info>. A successful response has type USERID with the printable user identifier. An error response has type ERROR with a reason code such as INVALID PORT, NO USER, or UNKNOWN ERROR. The server closes the connection after sending the response.
sections.plainLanguage: You send two port numbers to the server, and it replies with a name or an error message.

sections.title: Trustworthiness and Caveats
sections.content:
RFC 912 explicitly cautions that the trustworthiness of authentication servers varies widely. Different systems have different security policies and user identifier formats, and the information is only as reliable as the server that provides it. Implementations are advised to determine how much trust to place in returned identifiers.

The RFC suggests that use of the authentication service might be restricted to locally controlled subnets where administrators can verify the trustworthiness of the servers involved. Applications should not make security-critical decisions based solely on authentication service responses.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is only as trustworthy as the computer providing it. You have to decide whether you believe what it says.
